## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Garahitajātaka* (Ja 219), rendered in English as "Despised", is a birth story preserved in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative framework (*nidāna*), the Buddha related this story while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk afflicted with discontent and downcast in the religious life (*anabhiratiyā ukkaṇṭhita*) [Fausböll 1879; SuttaCentral]. The incipit of the story's verse begins *Hiraññam me suvaṇṇam me ti* ("The gold is mine...") [Fausböll 1879; SuttaCentral].
In the past-life narrative recounted by the Master, a certain location was scorned or despised, leading the characters to abandon it for another site, which gave rise to the place name *Garahitapiṭṭhipāsāṇa* [Fausböll 1879]. Upon the conclusion of the teaching of the Truths, the discontented monk attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) [Fausböll 1879]. In the closing identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha revealed that the troop of monkeys (*vānaragaṇa*) was the contemporary assembly of the Buddha (*Buddhaparisā*), while the monkey chief (*vānarinda*) was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1879].
No cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan collections are listed on SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus detects textual overlap exclusively within the Pali tradition, matching three passages with the commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (*Dutiyo bhāgo*), where the longest segment alignment (§1.1–2.6 with §1179–1184) exhibits a 0.93 similarity score [DharmaNexus].
